https://www.dw.com/en/who-is-responsible.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IH5r Spain dispatched the military to get the situation back under control Image: Henry Nicholls/AFP Advertisement For a long time, the Moroccan government chose not to comment on the Ceuta border crisis that saw tens of thousands of migrants surging into the Spanish exclave on the African continent. It was not until Sunday that Moroccan interior ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi said "the malicious exploitation of the digital space," "misleading information" and misinterpretations of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling were to blame for the incident. Morocco has since said it never intended for the border surge to happen and has promised full cooperation with Spain. Spain , however, was quick to suspect Moroccan involvement, with Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calling the border breach an "attack on our territorial sovereignty." Videos have, after all, surfaced showing Moroccan security forces doing nothing to stop the crowd surging forward. Efforts have been made to try and explain what caused the migrant crisis. Some have said Spain's recent rapprochement with Algeria may have angered Marocco, while others have speculated US influence may have played a role, although there is no reliable evidence to support the latter theory. A complex situation DW spoke with two analysts who caution against simplistic explanations. They do, however, ascribe different degrees of responsibility to Marocco for causing the crisis. "I think the situation today is significantly different from what it was in 2021," says Isabelle Werenfels, a Maghreb regional expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). Back then, Morocco was interested in exerting foreign policy pressure on Spain over the Western Sahara dispute, she says. Today, Morocco would have "a great deal to lose, above all, international credibility and investment" if found to have deliberately orchestrated the Ceuta migrant surge. Jochen Oltmer, a migration researcher at the University of Osnabrück in Germany, also warns against jumping to conclusions, telling DW "you have to keep in mind the many different interests at play." He points to Ceuta's unique status as a European exclave on the African continent, decades of migration flows, the impact of social networks, and the hopes of many migrants to build better lives abroad. A variety of factors account for the Ceuta migrant surge Image: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Oltmer says Moroccan authorities carry considerable responsibility for the Ceuta crisis, as "such a border crossing could never have taken place if the Moroccan side hadn't looked the other way." It was this inaction that made possible a border breach of this magnitude in the first place, he told DW. Werenfels does not dispute this assessment. Yet she also believes Morocco may have wanted to send a political signal to Spain, perhaps over its recent rapprochement with Algeria and its decision to grant Spanish citizenship to individuals born in Western Sahara before September 1977. Western Sahara: Caught between sovereignty and struggle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "But there is a significant difference between making a political statement and orchestrating a migration surge on this scale," Werenfels says. The expert thinks it is "unlikely" that Morocco had planned the latter, even though it cannot be ruled out, while stressing a lot of information remains extremely unclear- Who bears responsibility? There is some evidence to suggest that Morocco played a part in the border surge to push its own political agenda, says Oltmer. For years, the country has viewed itself as an indispensable partner to the European Union in the context of migration policy, he says, adding that Morocco has repeatedly emphasized how much the bloc depends on its cooperation. Yet the conflict over Western Sahara, and Morocco's rivalry with Algeria, also plays an important role, Oltmer explains. That is why he "ultimately cannot imagine that the recent events would have been possible without Morocco." Werenfels advocates for a more nuanced analysis. She suspects it's possible that Morocco wanted to send a message but that matters got out of control. Werenfels says it is hard to imagine that Morocco would want to risk a lasting rift with Spain and the European Union. This is all the more true given that Morocco will be hosting the next football World Cup together with Spain and Portugal, and also depends on Spanish gas supplies. In 2025, one-quarter of Spain's total natural gas exports went to Morocco. Even if Morocco had wanted to send a political message, that does not automatically mean that it deliberately orchestrated a migration surge of this magnitude, Werenfels says. Doing so would carry enormous political and economic risk. No evidence of third-party involvement Neither of the experts believe a third country played a part in the Ceuta migration crisis. That said, Werenfels does entertain the possibility that other governments or political actors may have attempted to exploit the situation propagandistically for their own political interests and thereby may have amplified the crisis. Werenfels also says it remains unclear how the situation escalated so quickly. There is much to suggest that news of an alleged border opening spread very quickly, prompting numerous young Moroccans to spontaneously set off for Ceuta. It is also possible that, given these circumstances, some Moroccan security personnel did not intervene. Both scholars agree on the root causes of migration. "It's about hope and expectations for the future," says Oltmer. Moroccans have been emigrating for many decades, with family and friendship networks in Europe making it easier for people to risk moving abroad, he says. Spanish soldiers escort migrants back to the border Image: Antonio Sempere/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Werenfels also points out social and economic factors driving emigration. She says that while Morocco had made progress in recent years, many young people are hardly seeing improvements in their everyday lives. The scholar says Marocco's education and health care sectors show particularly significant shortcomings. This lack of prospects compels many to risk migrating abroad, Werenfels says. Overall, both experts agree that the Ceuta migrant crisis was not brought about by a single political decision, or conspiracy theory, for that matter. The incident instead resulted from the interplay of geopolitical tensions, migration policy agendas, and the often precarious circumstances of many young Moroccans. We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.’ Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Edgars Rinkēvičs: ‘It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company. We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.’ Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Europe Latvia’s president warns that Europe is not up to date with drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine Edgars Rinkēvičs says drone warfare in Ukraine is moving at ‘lightning speed’ and efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by next year Andrew Roth in Washington Fri 18 Sep 2026 18.05 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Latvia’s president has warned that Europe is not keeping up with developments of drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine and that most countries in Nato could not repulse an attack by Russian missiles if the conflict expands. The remarks came during a Guardian interview in Washington DC in which Edgars Rinkēvičs said that the technological developments in drone warfare in Ukraine are moving at “lightning speed” and that current efforts to prepare for an aerial war could be obsolete by the middle of next year. “What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” he said. “And let’s be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and Nato has it. “Because if Russia decides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added. Ukraine and European allies are now facing a delay in supplies of crucial Patriot and other air-defence missiles. The US has expended nearly two-thirds of its stocks of critical interceptors in the war in Iran, according to analysis of a Congressional Budget Office assessment, and it could take at least five years to replenish stocks. The US has considered outsourcing Patriot production to Ukraine and Europe but so far an agreement has not been made. “It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company,” Rinkēvičs said, noting that discussions were continuing and acknowledging the difficulties of some technical issues with licensing. “We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.” At next week’s United Nations general assembly in New York City, Donald Trump is expected to hold meetings with senior European leaders, and as Nato allies have stepped up their warnings about the risk of Russia escalating the war in Ukraine. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned in a speech on Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against Nato countries supporting Ukraine in the coming months in an effort to test the alliance’s commitment to collective defence under article 5 of its charter. Tusk said that Russia would seek to “weaken Nato’s integrity” and show that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”, adding that Russia would seek to play off the incidents as accidents. Asked about Tusk’s concerns about Russia attacking Ukrainian allies in Europe, Trump said: “I think they already have attacked Ukrainian allies. They’ve been attacking Ukrainian allies for approximately five years.” He then pivoted to throw his support behind the Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, who is supported by the conservative Law and Justice party, saying: “You have a great president, he was a big Trump fan … he’s doing a fantastic job, and he’s got it under control.” The Baltic nations, which are also on Russia’s eastern flank, have tempered their warnings, saying that there was no indication that Moscow sought to launch a conventional war to retake territory that it once held under the Soviet Union. But Russia would increase mobilisation in the coming months after local elections, Rinkēvičs said, then use the winter to “push” in Ukraine, and also to “do whatever it takes to dissuade nations that are supportive of Ukraine to continue”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every fortnight Sign up to Global Dispatch Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team after newsletter promotion Acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and drone and missile incidents all indicated Russia testing European resolve to support Ukraine, he said. “I would rule out a conventional military incursion but we should be very vigilant when it comes to all kinds of other possibilities,” he said. A Nato jet shot down a Russian drone over Lithuania on Tuesday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and closed Lublin and Rzeszów-Jasionka airports on Thursday due to a Russian strike on western Ukraine. Rinkēvičs also expressed concern about whether European allies were on track to hit a goal of spending 5% of GDP on defence that has become a White House benchmark for the Trump administration’s continued support for Nato. He also said that discussions over Europe bearing a great burden for its own defence were growing “more constructive”, but added that when it comes to “real capabilities … you need time”. “Our message is also to do that, we need time,” he said. “It cannot happen in a month, or in a year.” Explore more on these topics Europe Latvia Ukraine Russia Drones (military) Nato news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says Trains carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials say Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe US envoys Kushner and Witkoff visit Kyiv for first time after Putin talks Witkoff and Kushner discussed ‘next steps’ with Putin to end Ukraine war, says US Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’ Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/liechten.text: Liechtenstein's Hereditary Prince Alois vetoed a bill on Tuesday that would have legalized abortion during the first 12 weeks of a woman's pregnancy, blocking a citizens' initiative co-signed by a quarter of voters and passed in the micro-state's parliament. Performing an abortion is currently illegal in the principality, unless the pregnancy presents a severe risk to the pregnant woman's health or if it is the result of a sexual assault. Women seeking an abortion usually travel to clinics in neighboring Austria or Switzerland, which campaigners say adds uncertainty and an unnecessary financial hurdle to the process. The bill was introduced by the Fristenlösung citizens' initiative, which collected almost 5,000 signatures — about a quarter of the state's registered voters. It proposed decriminalizing abortion up to 12 weeks' gestation, and to lift a ban on providing information about abortion. Advertisement Advertisement The bill "is not suitable for adequately protecting unborn life as a central legal interest," a statement from the princely house reads . Alois had already indicated in June he would veto the proposal on these grounds. "We're disappointed, but not really surprised," Tatjana As'Ad, a campaigner for the initiative and a co-managing director for the Free List, Liechtenstein's progressive opposition party, told POLITICO. "It was clear his decision was fixed in June and that there was no way we would change it." She added campaigners met Alois on Tuesday morning , but that there was no indication he would announce his veto shortly after. "We are frustrated because it feels like everything we did since June was decorative," As'Ad said. Liechtenstein, a small Alpine principality of about 40,000 people, has an atypical political system associating referendum-led direct democracy with a monarchy where the reigning prince retains extensive executive powers. Alois's absolute veto right was itself confirmed by a 2012 referendum. He used it for the first time to block the abortion bill. "The promise of dualism" between democracy and the monarchy "that the Liechtensteiners are trusting has got some cracks," As'Ad said. She added that the parliament's decision to vote through the bill and send it directly to Alois for assent, instead of calling for a referendum, "spared" the hereditary prince from a "conflict" with his people. Advertisement Advertisement She said her campaign's biggest win was a clarification from Liechtenstein's government that the ban on "information" about abortion was in effect a ban on "advertising" the practice. "In the end, everything is going to be the same," she said. "Women affected are still here. There is a majority in favor and it's still here. Abortions are still going to happen, and [Alois] just decided where they would be going to happen." Liechtenstein's princely house did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
